title: Phrasing spread of the four instruction conditions
takeaway: Across three task families and three models, a bare mention of the target puts it in the J-space almost as often as an explicit focus instruction, and forbidding the thought suppresses it barely at all; only the ignore framing, which calls the concept task-irrelevant, pushes the rate well down, and even then not to the no-instruction floor. Within every condition the individual phrasings spread widely, so the control the paper reports is real but phrasing-sensitive.
walkthrough:
This is the phrasing-level breakdown behind the [[directed-modulation]] result that Figure 10 summarizes. In the article it is a live widget titled "Directed modulation — robustness to prompt phrasing": a three-by-three grid of small panels, with a tooltip on every dot.

Columns are models, in ascending tiers of the [[claude-model-family]]: Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.5. Rows are task families. Category instance and math expression are versions of the [[hold-in-mind-copy-task]], where the model copies an unrelated sentence while an instruction says what to hold in mind, and the lens is read at the copied tokens. Line width is the [[character-counting-task]].

Each panel carries four bars, one per condition in the legend. A bar is the condition mean; the dots on it are the individual phrasings, five to eight per condition, hovering to reveal the template. Horizontal placement of a dot inside a bar is a fixed decorative offset and carries no information. The vertical axis runs from 0% to 100%. A thin horizontal rule marks the no-instruction floor.

The measure differs by row. Category and math count a trial as positive when the target reaches [[j-lens-readout]] top-1 at any (layer, position). Line width reports precision: the fraction of top-1 number tokens matching the true width.

Three patterns follow.

Mention nearly matches focus on the first two rows. On Opus, category runs 97.1% under focus against 87.2% under mention, and math runs 95.6% against 95.7% — mention is fractionally higher. Naming the concept at all loads it into the [[j-space]].

Don't-think suppresses very little: 83.1% on Opus category, 87.8% on Opus math, close to the mention rate. The paper reads this as a parallel to the human [[white-bear-effect]].

Ignore does suppress, to 46.6% and 41.4% on Opus, well below mention on every model, though still far above the floor of roughly 0% to 1.6%.

The line-width row behaves unlike the others. Only focus lifts it off the floor, and the phrasings scatter: on Opus, precision runs from 14.0% for "Focus on figuring out what that column number is" to 55.9% for "count the characters and keep the number in mind". The appendix attributes this to the task being harder both to perform and to specify.

terms.term: Directed modulation — robustness to prompt phrasing
terms.definition: The widget's own title. It states the question of the figure: whether the modulation effect reported in the main text survives changes in how the instruction is worded.

The workspace-like property under test: the claim that a model can deliberately place a concept into its workspace representation when told to, and reduce it when told to set it aside, independently of what it writes.

The instruction condition that tells the model to hold the target in mind while doing the cover task, for example "Concentrate on {x} while you write the sentence." One of the two conditions carried over from the main text.

The condition that names the target somewhere in the prompt with no instruction attached, for example "({x})" or "{x} came up in conversation." It isolates how much of the focus effect comes from the concept merely being present in context.

The condition that forbids the thought, for example "Whatever you do, do not think about {x}." It asks the model not to attend to the concept by prohibiting it rather than by calling it irrelevant. The article writes the name without an apostrophe in the legend and as don't-think in the caption.

The condition that frames the target as beside the point, for example "{x} is irrelevant to this task." The paper calls it dismissal in its data keys. It is the second of the two conditions reported in the main text.
The three production models the panels are computed on, in ascending size tier. Column position is the only place model identity appears.
The task family in which the model is told to hold in mind an item from a named category while copying an unrelated sentence. The target is the category instance the instruction names.
The task family in which the model mentally evaluates an arithmetic expression while copying an unrelated sentence. The target is the value of the expression.
The task family in which the model silently counts the characters on each line of a hard-wrapped passage while reading it. The target is the wrap width as a number.
The slot in a phrasing template where the trial's target is substituted: a category instance, a math expression, or, in the line-width templates, a description of the character count.
The concept the instruction is about on a given trial, and the thing the lens is checked for. A trial is scored by whether the target's token surfaces in the readout.

The Jacobian lens, the paper's read-out technique: for each vocabulary token it identifies the activation direction that encodes the model's potential to say that token, and scores every token against the current activation.
The single highest-scoring vocabulary token in a lens readout at one layer and one token position. The category and math panels score a trial positive if the target ever occupies that slot.

One cell of the grid the lens is applied over: a layer of the model crossed with a token position in the text being copied or read. "At any (layer, position)" means the target counts if it reaches top-1 in any of those cells.

terms.term: top-1 (metric label for the first two rows)
terms.definition: The scoring rule for the category and math rows: the fraction of trials on which the target reaches J-lens top-1 anywhere in the layer-by-position grid. It is a hit rate over trials, not an accuracy over readouts.

terms.term: precision (metric label for the line-width row)
terms.definition: The scoring rule for the line-width row: among readouts whose top-1 token is a number, the fraction that name the true wrap width. A model that never produces a numeric top-1 contributes nothing, so this measure is not comparable to the top-1 hit rate above it.
One run of a task family under one phrasing: a specific target, a specific carrier passage, and the instruction template filled in. Dot heights are rates over the trials for that phrasing.
The translucent bar behind the dots in each group, drawn at the mean rate across that condition's phrasings. The focus and ignore bars are the values plotted in the main-text figure.
One circle per instruction phrasing, placed at that phrasing's rate. Its horizontal offset within the bar is a fixed spacing device, not data.
The wording of one instruction, shown in the hover tooltip with {x} standing for the target, for example "Don't think about {x}." Each condition is instantiated with several of them.
The short internal name of a phrasing, shown above its template in the tooltip: foc_ for focus, men_ for mention, neg_ for don't-think, dis_ for ignore, and lb_ for the line-width variants.
The thin horizontal rule in each panel, marking the rate when the prompt gives no instruction and does not name the target. It is the reference for how much any condition adds.

The region of activation space spanned by sparse nonnegative combinations of J-lens vectors, which the paper argues functions as the model's global workspace. "The target is in the J-space" is what a top-1 hit is taken to indicate.
The human finding that being told to suppress a thought makes it occur more often than no instruction at all. The paper reads the don't-think bars sitting near the mention bars as a parallel.

The protocol behind the first two rows: the model copies an unrelated sentence while an instruction states what to hold in mind, and the lens is read at the copied tokens, where the surface text has nothing to do with the target.
The protocol behind the third row: the model reads a passage hard-wrapped to a fixed width and silently tracks the character count, with the lens read at the line-break positions.

numbers.meaning: Three task families crossed with three models. Every panel repeats the same four-bar structure, so a reader can compare any two cells directly.
focus, mention, don't-think and ignore. The main text reported only focus and ignore; mention and don't-think are added here to separate priming from prohibition.

numbers.value: five to eight phrasings per condition
numbers.meaning: The caption's stated range for how many wordings instantiate each condition. The counts in the data are 5 to 7 for the category and math rows, and 3 to 8 for the line-width row, where the mention condition has only three templates.
The vertical range of every panel, shared across all nine so heights are comparable. Category and math read as hit rates, line width as precision.
Category-instance focus means for Haiku, Sonnet, Opus. Told to hold the category instance in mind, all three models put it at J-lens top-1 on almost every trial, with a small rise across tiers.
Category-instance mention means. A bare naming of the target, with no instruction, already reaches most of the focus rate on Sonnet and Opus; the gap is wider on Haiku.

Category-instance don't-think means. They sit essentially on top of the mention means, which is what the paper points to as the white bear effect: forbidding the thought neither suppresses it nor, beyond the mention itself, inflates it.
Category-instance ignore means. Well below mention on all three models, so the irrelevance framing does pull the target down, but far above the no-instruction floor, so it does not remove it.
Math-expression focus means. The rate climbs steeply across the three tiers, more so than in the category row.
Math-expression mention means. On Sonnet and Opus these slightly exceed the focus means, so on this task an explicit instruction adds nothing measurable over naming the expression.
Math-expression don't-think means. Below mention but not far below, and rising with model tier.
Math-expression ignore means. Roughly half the mention rate on the two larger models and about a fifth of it on Haiku.

Line-width focus means, as precision. Much lower than the other two rows and not monotonic in model size: Sonnet scores above Opus. The appendix ascribes the difference to the task being harder to perform and harder to specify.
Line-width mention means. Naming the wrap without asking for the count leaves precision at a few percent, close to the floor, so the priming seen in the other rows does not appear here.
Line-width don't-think means, again near the floor.
Line-width ignore means, at or below the floor line for that panel.

The no-instruction floors drawn as the horizontal rule in each of the nine panels. They are the paper's evidence that context alone does not place the target in the readout, which is why any bar above them is attributed to the instruction.

The spread of the seven don't-think phrasings on Haiku, category instance. The low end is "Don't worry about {x}." and the high end "Whatever you do, do not think about {x}.", so the same nominal condition covers a five-fold range.
The spread of the six mention phrasings on Haiku, category instance. The bare parenthetical "({x})" primes hardest; the buried "There is a phrase, {x}, included here." primes least.
The spread of the six ignore phrasings on Opus, math expression. "{x} is irrelevant — ignore it." suppresses most; "{x} is unrelated to this task." suppresses least.

The spread of the five line-width focus phrasings on Opus, quoted in the appendix text as 14% to 56%. The oblique "Focus on figuring out what that column number is while you read." sits at the bottom and the direct "At each line break, count the characters and keep the number in mind." at the top, which is the paper's evidence that the specification, not only the task, is doing the work.
